995.title: Mary, Help of Christians (24 May)
995.hook: a title loved by John Bosco and Australian Catholics
995.howItsDone: Catholics invoke Mary as Help of Christians in the Litany of Loreto; the Salesians of John Bosco and the Church in Australia keep 24 May as a special feast, and the invocation 'Mary, Help of Christians, pray for us' is a common short prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mexican martyrs, and Father Magallanes forgiving the men in front of him. Your line was long live christ the king. When did you answer without hatred? Day nine hundred ninety-five.

A wedding in Cana. The party is in full swing, and somewhere near the kitchen the wine has just run out. Out of wine, in front of every guest. The couple may not know yet. But one guest does. She doesn't make a scene. She walks over to her son and says four plain words. That's it. No speech, no plan, just the problem, handed to the one who can do something about it. Today, a title Catholics give that guest. Mary, Help of Christians.
screen: `A WEDDING IN CANA.` → `THE WINE RUNS OUT.` → `ONE GUEST NOTICES.`

segments.voice: Here's what she says, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." She notices a need before anyone asks, and she brings it to Jesus. Then she turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Catholics see in this scene the whole shape of Mary's help. She notices. She brings the need to her son. And she points people back to him. Help of Christians is one of the titles Catholics call her by in the Litany of Loreto, a long prayer of names for Mary, each followed by the words pray for us. The title has been prayed in hard times: by people under threat, by people in exile, by a Church in trouble. Tradition ties it to moments when Catholics believed her prayers had helped them through danger. Then there's John Bosco, the Italian priest who gave his life to poor and abandoned boys in Turin. He loved this title and built a church in Turin under it, and tradition says he credited Mary, Help of Christians, with what his work achieved. His followers carried the devotion far beyond Turin. In Australia, Catholics honor Mary under this title as the patron of their country. Catholics and other Christians differ on how to speak of Mary. Catholics, like Orthodox Christians, ask for her prayers, while Protestant churches generally address prayer to God alone. For Catholics, her help is never separate from Christ. It's what she did at Cana: noticing, asking him, and saying, do what he tells you.
screen: `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `SHE NOTICES, ASKS, POINTS TO HIM.` · `A TITLE FROM THE LITANY.` · `JOHN BOSCO, TURIN, AUSTRALIA.` · then, large: `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the empty jar. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that has run out. Patience at home. Money at the end of the month. Hope for someone you love. Say it as plainly as Mary did: they have no wine; I have no patience; she has no hope. If you pray, you can use the line from the litany: Help of Christians, pray for us. If you don't, simply name what's empty, and sit with it honestly, without dressing it up. The bell holds the time.
Mary. Under the title Help of Christians: the one who noticed the wine was gone at Cana, and told the servants to do what her son said.
Your line: help of christians. Today, notice one need before anyone asks, and quietly bring it to someone who can help. Day nine hundred ninety-five.

996.title: The Visitation (31 May)
996.hook: May ends where Mary's traveling began, with Elizabeth
996.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Visitation on 31 May, closing the month Catholic tradition dedicates to Mary; Elizabeth's greeting is prayed in every Hail Mary, and the Magnificat is sung at Evening Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary, Help of Christians, the guest at Cana who noticed the wine was gone. Your line was help of christians. What need did you notice before anyone asked? Day nine hundred ninety-six.

A young woman has just heard news that will change everything. An angel, Luke says, has told her she will bear a son. And in the same breath, the angel mentions her older relative Elizabeth, who was called barren, and who is now with child too. What does she do next? She doesn't sit at home with the secret. She doesn't wait to be sure. She packs and goes, up into the hill country, to the one other woman who might understand. Today, the last feast of May. The Visitation.
screen: `NEWS THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING.` → `ELIZABETH IS WITH CHILD TOO.` → `SHE PACKS AND GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's how Luke puts it, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda." With haste. Mary doesn't drift. She goes. Then the arrival. Mary walks in and greets Elizabeth, and Luke says the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out with a loud voice: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Those words may sound familiar. Catholics say them in the Hail Mary, after the angel's greeting, so they pray this meeting every time they say it. Notice who is in the room. Two women, one old and one young, both carrying children nobody expected. No priests, no crowds, no kings. Two relatives in a house in the hills, and the one Luke says leaped for joy is a child not yet born. Then Mary answers with a song of her own, the one Catholics call the Magnificat and still sing at evening prayer. And she stays. Luke says about three months. Not a quick visit and a gift at the door. Luke doesn't say what filled those months; tradition pictures her helping as Elizabeth's time drew near. That's the shape of the feast. Good news doesn't make Mary sit still. It sends her out, fast, to someone who needs company, and once she's there, she doesn't hurry away.
screen: `MARY GOES WITH HASTE.` · `THE CHILD LEAPS.` · `BLESSED ART THOU AMONG WOMEN.` · `SHE STAYS ABOUT THREE MONTHS.` · then, large: `SHE WENT IN HASTE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go soon, and stay. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who might need company right now. Someone expecting a child, or caring for one. Someone older, living alone. Someone in the middle of news they haven't told many people. Notice what has kept you from going: waiting for a better week, waiting to know what to say. Mary didn't wait. Choose the soonest real moment you could be with them. Then choose one way to stay longer than usual: the phone put away, no glance at the clock. If you pray, you can say the words Elizabeth said, the ones Catholics say in the Hail Mary. If you don't, simply hold that person in mind. The bell holds the time.
The Visitation. Mary's journey into the hill country to visit Elizabeth, where the child leaped and Elizabeth called her blessed.
Your line: she went in haste. Today, visit someone, or call and set a date, and when you go, don't rush away. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: Kevin of Glendalough (3 June)
997.hook: an Irish hermit who, legend says, held still while a blackbird nested in his hand
997.howItsDone: Saint Kevin is remembered on 3 June, above all in Ireland; pilgrims visit the monastic site at Glendalough, and the blackbird story is often told or shown in pictures of him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Visitation: Mary hurrying over the hills to her cousin Elizabeth. Your line was she went in haste. Where did you hurry toward someone, and not away? Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

A stone cell in a wooded Irish valley. A man kneels inside, praying, with one arm stretched out through the small window, palm up, as still as a branch. A blackbird lands on the open hand. She looks around. She starts to bring twigs, one at a time. Yesterday was all haste. Today, the opposite: an Irish saint whose story is about not moving at all. Today, Kevin of Glendalough.
screen: `A STONE CELL IN A VALLEY.` → `AN ARM THROUGH THE WINDOW.` → `A BLACKBIRD LANDS.`

segments.voice: Start with what is history and what is legend. Kevin was a hermit and a monk in Ireland, and the monastery that grew up around him in the valley of Glendalough is remembered as his. The blackbird comes from the legend. It was written down long after his time, by medieval writers including Gerald of Wales, and it goes like this. Kevin was praying with one hand stretched out through the window of his cell, and a blackbird built a nest in his upturned palm and laid her eggs there. And Kevin did not pull his hand back. Tradition says he held it there, patient, until the eggs hatched and the young birds flew. Nobody has to believe a man held his arm out that long to hear what the story is saying. It is a picture of prayer as staying. Not prayer as getting something done, but prayer as being so still that a living thing can trust you with its future. The psalm says it in a single line. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be still and see that I am God." Kevin's hand is that line made into a scene. Notice what the story counts as holy. Not a miracle Kevin performs. A small bird's ordinary work, nest and eggs and feeding, which he refuses to interrupt. In stories like this one, animals are treated as neighbors in God's world. Jesus points at birds too. "Behold the birds of the air," he says, and reminds his listeners that their heavenly Father feeds them. Kevin does more than look. He becomes the place the bird is fed. And here is the hard edge of it. Holding still costs something. An arm gets tired. A plan gets canceled. Some readers hear the story as being about anyone who stays put for someone else's sake: a parent by a crib, a nurse by a bed, a friend who doesn't leave the room.
screen: `HISTORY: A HERMIT IN A VALLEY.` · `LEGEND: A NEST IN HIS OPEN HAND.` · `PRAYER AS STAYING.` · `HOLDING STILL COSTS SOMETHING.` · then, large: `BE STILL AND SEE THAT I AM GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold still for a minute. Sit, and rest one hand on your knee, palm up, open. Don't grip anything. Let the hand be a place where something could land. Breathe. When you want to shift, notice the wanting, and stay a little longer. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line once, slowly: be still and see that I am God. If you don't pray, simply let the open hand be enough. Then let the stillness run on. The bell holds the time.
Kevin, the Irish hermit of Glendalough. Legend says he held his hand still until a blackbird's young had flown.
Your line: the blackbird. Today, when someone starts talking to you, stop what your hands are doing and stay with them until they're finished. Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

998.title: Norbert (6 June)
998.hook: a courtier knocked from his horse by lightning who founded the Premonstratensians
998.howItsDone: Saint Norbert is remembered on 6 June; the Norbertine (Premonstratensian) canons and their parishes and schools keep it as their founder's feast, often with Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours sung together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kevin of Glendalough, and the bird in his open hand. Your line was the blackbird. Who did you stay still for? Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

Lightning, on a country road. Below it, a rider in fine clothes, on his way somewhere that matters to him. The storm breaks right overhead. A bolt strikes the ground in front of the horse, the horse rears, and the rider is thrown into the mud. He lies there, stunned, rain on his face, and, the story goes, he hears a voice. Yesterday's saint never moved. Today's saint gets moved, hard. Today, Norbert.
screen: `A RIDER IN FINE CLOTHES.` → `LIGHTNING ON THE ROAD.` → `THROWN INTO THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Norbert was a nobleman and a cleric at court, in the German lands, with a comfortable life and good connections. Tradition remembers him as worldly: holding church positions without much interest in what they were for. Then came the storm. In the story, as he lay on the ground he asked what Paul had asked: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" And the answer that came back was a line from a psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "Turn away from evil and do good." No vision of angels, no long speech. A line he would have known by heart, suddenly aimed at him. The scene has an echo. Paintings show Paul thrown from a horse on the road to Damascus. But read Acts, and there's no horse. The Douay-Rheims says only: "And falling on the ground, he heard a voice." The horse comes from the painters. Norbert's story has a real one, and the echo is hard to miss. What did Norbert do with it? He didn't change overnight into someone else. He did penance, was ordained a priest, and started preaching, barefoot, tradition says, from town to town. Then, at a remote place in France called Prémontré, he gathered men to live as canons: priests who pray the hours together like monks but go out to serve parishes. From that place comes the long name of his order, the Premonstratensians. They're also called, more simply, the Norbertines. Later he became an archbishop and worked to reform the clergy, the very kind of comfortable churchman he had once been. In Norbert's story, conversion is not one bright moment, but a fall, a question, and a long life of answering it.
screen: `A COMFORTABLE COURTIER.` · `THE QUESTION: WHAT WILT THOU HAVE ME DO?` · `PAUL'S HORSE IS NOT IN ACTS.` · `A FALL, THEN A LONG ANSWER.` · then, large: `TURN AWAY FROM EVIL AND DO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish someone a good turning. Not an argument to win, just a turning you'd hope for them. Close your eyes for a moment. Bring to mind one person caught in something that's hurting them, or a habit, or a hardness. Maybe it's you. Hold them without lecturing. If you pray, you can ask quietly, as Norbert did, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? and leave space for an answer. If you don't, simply wish them a good turning, in their own time. The bell holds the time.
Norbert. A courtier thrown to the ground in a storm, who turned, preached, and founded the Norbertines at Prémontré.
Your line: knocked from his horse. Today, when something knocks your plans over, before you get back up, ask what it might be asking of you. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

999.title: Barnabas (11 June)
999.hook: son of encouragement, who vouched for Paul when no one else would
999.howItsDone: The Church keeps the memorial of Saint Barnabas, Apostle, on 11 June; at Mass the readings come from Acts, where Barnabas is sent out with Saul from Antioch.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Norbert, thrown into the mud by a storm. Your line was knocked from his horse. When your plans fell over, what did you hear? Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

They were all afraid of him, Acts says. Not long ago he was hunting them. He dragged believers out of their houses. Now he has come to Jerusalem saying he has met the risen Jesus on the road. The disciples don't believe he is one of them. Nobody moves toward him. And then one man takes him, and brings him to the apostles, and speaks for him. Today, the man who helped another one stand. Barnabas.
screen: `A ROOM FULL OF FRIGHTENED PEOPLE.` → `A FORMER PERSECUTOR AT THE DOOR.` → `ONE MAN STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: Barnabas wasn't even his first name. Acts introduces him as Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas. And Acts translates it for us. In the Douay-Rheims: "The son of consolation." Newer translations say son of encouragement. The Greek word behind it, paraklēsis, can mean comfort, encouragement, or an appeal. A nickname like that is given, not chosen. The first thing we see him do is give: he sells a piece of land and lays the money at the apostles' feet. The second is the scene from the hook. Saul, later called Paul, comes to Jerusalem after his conversion, and the disciples are afraid of him. Acts says they did not believe he was a disciple. Then: "But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles." He tells them Saul's story, the road, the voice, the bold preaching in Damascus. He puts his own name behind a man nobody trusted. Later, when the church at Antioch is growing, it's Barnabas they send, and Acts gives him a one-line portrait: "For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith." And what does he do there? He goes looking for Saul and brings him to Antioch to teach. Again. Acts is honest that encouragers can disagree. Later Barnabas wants to give a young man named John Mark a second chance after he had left them partway through a journey. Paul refuses. The disagreement is sharp, and they part ways. Barnabas takes Mark anyway. Catholics remember Barnabas as an apostle, though he wasn't one of the Twelve. His gift was seeing what someone could become, and saying so out loud, before anyone else would.
screen: `JOSEPH, NICKNAMED BARNABAS.` · `HE VOUCHES FOR SAUL.` · `A GOOD MAN, FULL OF FAITH.` · `A SECOND CHANCE FOR MARK.` · then, large: `THE SON OF CONSOLATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: vouch for someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person others have written off, or who's new and unsure, or who's trying to start over. Picture them waiting at the edge of a room. Now picture yourself walking over and standing next to them. What would you say about them, honestly, that's good? Find the words. If you pray, you can hold them before God as Barnabas held Saul up before the apostles. If you don't, simply keep their good in mind. The bell holds the time.
Barnabas. The apostles' nickname for Joseph of Cyprus, the son of consolation, who brought Saul in when no one else would.
Your line: son of encouragement. Today, say one good thing about someone to a person who matters to them, while they can hear it, or pass it on later. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

1000.title: Anthony of Padua (13 June)
1000.hook: a great Franciscan preacher, now asked to find lost things
1000.howItsDone: The Church keeps the memorial of Saint Anthony of Padua on 13 June; Catholics ask his intercession when something is lost, and some parishes bless and hand out bread on his feast, called Saint Anthony's bread, for the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barnabas, who walked Saul into a room that feared him. Your line was son of encouragement. Whose good did you say out loud? Day one thousand.

Keys. Glasses. A ring. A passport the night before a flight. Somewhere, right now, someone is turning a couch cushion over again and saying, half joking and half not, Saint Anthony, help. Day one thousand on this path, and the saint for it is one whose name gets said in kitchens and parking lots. But that's not how he started. He started as a voice that filled a square. Today, Anthony of Padua.
screen: `KEYS. GLASSES. A RING.` → `SAINT ANTHONY, HELP.` → `A VOICE THAT FILLED A SQUARE.`

segments.voice: Anthony was born in Lisbon, in Portugal, and became a canon, then a Franciscan friar, drawn to the order of Francis of Assisi while Francis was still alive. He hoped to go to Morocco as a missionary. Illness sent him back, a storm blew his ship off course, and he ended up in Italy, an unknown friar. Then one day, the story goes, at an ordination, no one was ready to preach, and Anthony was told to say something. He opened his mouth, and the room discovered he knew the Scriptures deeply. From then on he preached across Italy and France, to crowds that filled churches and spilled into squares. The Church later named him a Doctor of the Church. So how does a great preacher become the saint of lost keys? The story tradition tells is small. Tradition says a young friar who was leaving the order took Anthony's book of psalms with him, a book Anthony had filled with notes for his preaching. Anthony prayed for it. The young man returned the book, and came back to the community too. Something precious was lost, and found, and a person along with it. That's an old pattern in the Gospels. Jesus tells of a woman who sweeps her whole house for one silver coin, and when she finds it she calls in the neighbors. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice with me, because I have found the groat which I had lost." In Catholic teaching, asking Anthony's help isn't a lucky charm. It's asking a friend in heaven to pray with you, as you'd ask a friend at the table. And some pray to him for things bigger than keys: a lost faith, a lost child, a friendship gone quiet.
screen: `FROM LISBON TO AN UNKNOWN FRIAR.` · `THE PREACHER NO ONE EXPECTED.` · `THE BOOK OF PSALMS, RETURNED.` · `A FRIEND ASKED TO PRAY WITH YOU.` · then, large: `I HAVE FOUND THE GROAT WHICH I HAD LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for something lost. Settle, and breathe. Let one lost thing come to mind. Maybe it's small and annoying. Maybe it's not a thing at all: a habit of prayer, a person you've drifted from, a version of yourself you miss. Name it plainly, once. Don't search yet. Just hold it, the way the woman lit her candle before she swept. If you pray, you can ask Saint Anthony to pray with you for it. If you don't, simply let yourself admit you'd like it back. The bell holds the time.
Padua, the Italian city linked to the Franciscan preacher Anthony, born in Lisbon, now asked by Catholics to help them find what's lost.
Your line: finder of lost things. Today, help someone else find something, or reach out once to someone you've lost touch with. Day one thousand.

1001.title: Aloysius Gonzaga (21 June)
1001.hook: a young Jesuit who died nursing plague victims in Rome
1001.howItsDone: The Church keeps the memorial of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga on 21 June; Jesuit schools and parishes often mark it, and he is honored as a patron of young people and students.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony of Padua, the preacher people call on for lost things. Your line was finder of lost things. What did you help someone find? Day one thousand one.

Look back over this week. Mary, Help of Christians. Mary hurrying to Elizabeth. Kevin with a bird in his hand. Norbert in the mud. Barnabas bringing Saul in. Anthony and a lost book. Holding still, turning, vouching, finding. Today the week ends in a crowded hospital in Rome, during an epidemic, where, the story goes, a young Jesuit stoops to lift a sick man off the street and carry him inside. Today, Aloysius Gonzaga.
screen: `A WEEK: STILL, TURNED, VOUCHED, FOUND.` → `A CROWDED HOSPITAL IN ROME.` → `A YOUNG MAN LIFTS A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Aloysius was born into the Gonzagas, a powerful noble family in northern Italy. He was the eldest son, the heir. His father wanted a soldier and a prince, and trained him for it. Aloysius wanted something else. Tradition says he was serious about prayer from childhood, and that as a teenager at court he decided to join the Jesuits. His father fought it for a long time. In the end Aloysius signed away his inheritance to his younger brother and walked into the Jesuit novitiate in Rome with nothing that marked him as a prince. Then came the epidemic. Rome was full of the sick, and the Jesuits went out to nurse them. Aloysius asked to go. He washed and fed the sick, made their beds, carried them. One story told about him is that he found a man collapsed in the street, lifted him onto his shoulders and brought him to the hospital. He caught the disease himself, and after a long illness he died, still young, still a student, not yet a priest. Jesus describes the judgment of the nations, and among the things the righteous did, he lists this. In the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me." Aloysius took it literally, and it cost him his life. Pictures of him often show a lily, a sign of purity, and a pale, pious face. That image can make him look fragile. The story says something tougher. A young man who stood up to a powerful father, gave away a fortune, and walked toward a disease many were running from. The Church named him a patron of young people, and the story behind the title isn't gentleness. It's a young man, and a brave one.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for the sick, starting in your mind. Let your hands rest. Bring to mind someone who is ill right now: at home, in a hospital, or simply worn out and unwell. And then the people caring for them: a nurse on a long shift, a parent up at night, an aide nobody thanks. Hold both. If you pray, you can ask Saint Aloysius to stay close to them. If you don't, simply think of one small thing you could do for one of them this week. The bell holds the time.
Aloysius Gonzaga. The heir who gave up a princely life to be a Jesuit, and died young after nursing the sick of Rome.
